# ECON 0100 | Homework C3 | Corrective Policies

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

*Answers and work are shown in the red blocks.*

## Q1 | Malodorous Byproducts

Butterbeer is beloved by Hogwarts students and teachers alike and is widely available at wizarding shops. But the beverage has the negative effect of generating displeasing odors from its imbibers. Preferences for butterbeer and its marginal cost can be represented by the following relationships.

$$
D: P_B = 40 - Q_D \qquad\qquad S: P_S = 10 + \frac{1}{2} Q_S
$$

Prices are in galleons and quantity is in bottles. The odor imposes a cost of 9 galleons per bottle on everyone nearby.

Using your economic policy advising credentials, offer a remedy to the malodorous byproduct the Ministry could implement. And conclude with a description of the effects your policy would have on the butterbeer market.

Policy (tax or subsidy): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Size per bottle: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Market Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Quantity with Your Policy: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::::: solution

Policy: a per-unit (corrective, or Pigouvian) tax. Size: $9$ galleons per bottle. Market quantity: $20$ bottles. Quantity with your policy: $14$ bottles.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

**Market.** Buyers and sellers ignore the odor, so the market settles where demand meets supply:

$$
40 - Q = 10 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 20, \quad P = 20
$$

**Efficient quantity.** Each bottle costs the brewer $10 + \frac{1}{2} Q$ and costs everyone nearby $9$ more, so the marginal social cost is $\text{MSC} = 19 + \frac{1}{2} Q$. Society wants bottles only while their marginal benefit covers that:

$$
40 - Q = 19 + \tfrac{1}{2} Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 14
$$

:::

::: column

![Corrective tax](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

**Why a tax of 9.** The market overproduces because sellers leave $9$ of each bottle’s cost out of their decision. A tax of exactly $9$ per bottle hands that cost back to them: to sell a bottle they now need its private cost *plus* $9$, which is the marginal social cost. The market then stops where marginal benefit equals marginal social cost, the same quantity a social planner would choose. The tax wedge of $9$ only fits between demand and supply at $Q = 14$.

**Effects on the market** (for reference; not asked). Buyers pay $40 - 14 = 26$, up $6$; sellers keep $10 + 7 = 17$, down $3$; the Ministry collects $9 \times 14 = 126$. Bottles $15$ through $20$ cost society more than they are worth to buyers, so the market quantity carried a deadweight loss, the gray triangle between MSC and demand:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9 \times (20 - 14) = 27
$$

The tax eliminates it. The odor still exists, but only on bottles worth their full cost.

:::::

\newpage

How does your policy bring the market to the socially efficient quantity?

> a\) It shifts supply down by the external cost, so sellers offer more bottles at every price.
>
> b\) Sellers now pay the odor’s cost on every bottle, so their cost plus the tax matches marginal social cost, and the market settles where marginal benefit equals marginal social cost.
>
> c\) It caps the price of butterbeer, so sellers make fewer bottles.
>
> d\) The Ministry pays the revenue to everyone nearby, which removes the odor.

::: solution

**b)**

The tax raises the cost sellers face on every bottle by the odor’s $9$, so supply plus the tax is MSC and the market lands where $\text{MB} = \text{MSC}$. a) has the shift backwards: a tax shifts the sellers’ curve up, and the market needs fewer bottles, not more. c) is a price ceiling, which is not the policy. d) What the Ministry does with the revenue does not change the quantity; the tax works by making sellers face the cost.

:::

\newpage

## Q2 | Dragon Pox

Dragon Pox is spreading through the wizarding world. A dose of Gorsemoor’s Draught keeps a witch or wizard from catching it, so whoever drinks it also can’t pass Dragon Pox on to anyone else. The marginal private benefit of a dose is $P = 24 - Q$, and supply, which is both the private and the social cost, is $P = 4 + Q$. Prices are in galleons and quantity is in doses. Each dose also gives a benefit of 6 galleons to everyone else, since they are less likely to catch Dragon Pox.

Offer a remedy the Ministry could implement to correct the market failure. And conclude with a description of the effects your policy would have on the market for Gorsemoor’s Draught.

Policy (tax or subsidy): \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Size per dose: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Market Quantity: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ Quantity with Your Policy: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::::: solution

Policy: a per-unit (corrective, or Pigouvian) subsidy. Size: $6$ galleons per dose. Market quantity: $10$ doses. Quantity with your policy: $13$ doses.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: column

**Market.** Buyers count only their own benefit, so the market settles where marginal private benefit meets supply:

$$
24 - Q = 4 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 10, \quad P = 14
$$

**Efficient quantity.** Each dose is worth $24 - Q$ to the drinker and $6$ more to everyone else, so the marginal social benefit is $\text{MSB} = 30 - Q$. Society wants doses as long as that covers the cost:

$$
30 - Q = 4 + Q \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 13
$$

:::

::: column

![Corrective subsidy](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

**Why a subsidy of 6.** The market underproduces because buyers leave the $6$ of benefit to everyone else out of their decision. A subsidy of exactly $6$ per dose pays them that benefit: a dose is now worth its private benefit *plus* $6$ to the buyer, which is the marginal social benefit. The market then stops where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost, the same quantity a social planner would choose. The subsidy wedge of $6$ only fits between supply and demand at $Q = 13$.

**Effects on the market** (for reference; not asked). Buyers pay $24 - 13 = 11$, down $3$; sellers receive $4 + 13 = 17$, up $3$; the Ministry spends $6 \times 13 = 78$. Doses $11$ through $13$ are worth more to society than they cost, so the market quantity carried a deadweight loss, the gray triangle between MSB and supply:

$$
\text{DWL} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times (13 - 10) = 9
$$

The subsidy eliminates it.

:::::

How does your policy bring the market to the socially efficient quantity?

> a\) It lowers the cost of brewing each dose, so sellers offer fewer.
>
> b\) It raises the price buyers pay, so fewer witches and wizards drink it.
>
> c\) Buyers now receive the benefit to everyone else on every dose, so their benefit plus the subsidy matches marginal social benefit, and the market settles where marginal social benefit equals marginal cost.
>
> d\) It sets a price floor, so sellers earn more on every dose.

::: solution

**c)**

The subsidy adds the $6$ of benefit to everyone else to what each dose is worth to its buyer, so demand plus the subsidy is MSB and the market lands where $\text{MSB} = \text{MC}$. a) A lower cost would mean *more* doses, not fewer. b) The subsidy lowers the price buyers pay, from $14$ to $11$, so more of them drink it. d) is a price floor, which is not the policy.

:::
